_comment: Per-finding gosec waivers for code outside Phase 0/Part 0 (W1-W6)/Phase 1 scope, per the Phase 0 CI harness item's pre-existing-findings policy (.SPECIFICATION/IMPLEMENTATION.md). Every entry names one exact (file, line, rule) finding gosec currently reports and a reason; it is not a blanket rule or directory exclusion. A finding that stops matching (because the surrounding code moved) must be re-reviewed, not silently re-added: that is deliberate, not a maintenance burden to route around. Every entry's backstop is AGENTS.md's actual rule, quoted in full: 'gosec and govulncheck must be validated prior to production packaging (Phase 20).' CORRECTED TWICE on 2026-08-15, and the second correction is the one that matters. This header used to assert that AGENTS.md required ZERO REMAINING WAIVERS before Phase 20. It does not, and never did; the sentence above is AGENTS.md's only rule on the subject and it says nothing about waiver counts. The zero-waiver bar was written into Phase 0's pre-existing-findings policy, copied into this header, and attributed in both places to AGENTS.md, so removing it is deleting a misquotation rather than a phase relaxing a project rule it was measured against. Both copies were struck on the same day; the Phase 0 one is the origin. UPDATED 2026-08-15 by Phase 20b, which is the entry that paid the promise off: the three insecure-cookie entries (G124, CookieCodec.writeInsecure, Handler.writeInsecurePreference, Handler.writeInsecurePreAuthCookie) are GONE, removed with the code they guarded rather than re-waived, because the controller now terminates TLS and refuses to serve plain HTTP unattended (cmd/controller's resolveTLS). Twelve entries became nine and the whole cookie class is closed. What the nine are: one G705 in internal/api/logs.go, three G710 open-redirect entries in internal/ui/web/auth.go (whose lines moved when the insecure writer was deleted from that file, so each was re-reviewed against unchanged code and renumbered, never silently re-added), three G101 heuristic matches on the word 'credential' in a scope name and a form-field prefix, one G101 on an AWX endpoint name, and one G204 in internal/testsupport's docker build helper. Seven of the nine name Phase 39 as re-verifier and Phase 39 has closed, so Phase 82 was appended to own them rather than leaving a stale pointer; two are test-only (tests/parity/awx.go, internal/testsupport/ansible_image.go) and guard no shipping artifact, which is machine-checkable and true even though gosec-check itself draws no such boundary. One caveat this file has always understated, re-measured on the same day: it is the SMALLER of two suppression channels. Inline '#nosec' comments account for 56 further suppressions that never appear here, which is gosec's own Stats.nosec under the exact command tools/gosec-check runs, so this file's nine entries are about 14 percent of the project's suppressed findings rather than all of them. That count went UP by one in Phase 20b even while three waivers were deleted: the container healthcheck reads its own TLS_CERT_FILE to verify the local listener, which is a G304 the same shape internal/crypto's key_resolve.go already carries, so the honest summary of that phase is three waivers and one class removed, one inline suppression added. Quote the 56 with its method, because it is fragile: 67 raw lines match a grep for the string, 56 are suppressions under this project's invocation, and 101 if -tests is added, which tools/gosec-check does not pass. The bar Phase 20 was held to was zero remaining waivers OF THE COOKIE CLASS, and it is met. Nothing here sets a project-wide zero-waiver deadline, because no phase owns one; if that bar is wanted it needs a phase behind it, not a sentence. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-16 by Phase 20f, the pass that narrowed internal/tlscert's ownership rule to the one thing it protects, and this measurement supersedes every one below it. Nine waivers, unchanged and unmoved: no guarded line shifted, so nothing needed re-review, and the nine are the same nine listed above. Zero G124. The inline count reads 58 under the exact command tools/gosec-check runs, up one from 57, and the one is this pass: internal/tlscert/read.go's existing G304 is unchanged, and the new suppression is in cmd/controller/servingcert_race_test.go, on the exec.Command that starts the long-lived child for TestARunningControllerSurvivesASiblingsRenewal. It is the same shape as the two that file already carries and the reason is the same one: the program is os.Executable() and the only argument is a fixed -test.run flag, so nothing in it comes from input. Two suppressions were AVOIDED rather than written and both are worth recording. The new private-key detection parses candidate DER through crypto/x509 rather than shelling out to openssl, so there is no G204 anywhere near the decision that protects a secret. And the refusal messages name the running user through os.Geteuid rather than reading /etc/passwd or an environment variable, so no file is opened to build an error string and no G304 arises on a path that only exists to be printed. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-15 by Phase 20e, the pass that replaced the certificate claim lock with a design that has no lock, and this measurement supersedes the ones below it. Nine waivers, unchanged and unmoved: no guarded line shifted, so nothing needed re-review, and the nine are the same nine listed above. Zero G124. The inline count still reads 57 under the exact command tools/gosec-check runs, and it is worth saying what did NOT change it, since this pass added three suppressions and removed three. Added: two G204 in cmd/controller's new servingcert_race_test.go and one more in internal/tlscert's concurrent_test.go, each on an exec.Command whose program is os.Executable() and whose only argument is a fixed -test.run flag, which is how both packages start real processes to race each other over one directory. Removed: the two that Phase 20d recorded as deliberately AVOIDED are gone along with the code that avoided them, and the sentence recording them is now history rather than description. There is no generation lock to be an os.Mkdir instead of an O_CREATE|O_EXCL open, and no retry schedule to be jittered with crypto/rand instead of math/rand, because there is no retry: a controller loads what is published, writes one file if it has to, and loads again. The NFS reasoning that chose mkdir is not lost, it is satisfied more cheaply, since rename(2) is atomic everywhere that matters and every write in internal/tlscert is now a rename of a file no other writer names. tools/devcert and tools/uidev moved from //go:build ignore to //go:build devtools in the same pass and are compiled and vetted by `make ci`; gosec is still run with no -tags, so neither is scanned and neither adds a finding, which is the same boundary the ignore tag drew and the reason the tag was kept rather than deleted. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-15 by Phase 20d, the adversarial-fix pass over 20b and 20c, and this is the measurement that supersedes the two below it. Nine waivers, unchanged and unmoved: no guarded line shifted, so nothing needed re-review, and the nine are the same nine listed above. Zero G124, which is the bar Phase 20 was actually held to. The inline count reads 57 under the exact command tools/gosec-check runs, up one from 56, and NONE of that one is this pass: internal/tlscert/read.go gained a G304 for reading certificate material through a guard that refuses anything which is not an ordinary file, and cmd/controller/healthcheck.go LOST the G304 20b added, because the probe no longer reads its own certificate file at all and asks internal/tlscert for its trust anchors instead. One in, one out, net zero. The 57th belongs to the Helm chart work landing alongside this one (tools/helm-lint/main.go's G204 on a fixed "helm" literal), so a later reader comparing counts should attribute it there rather than here. Two further suppressions were AVOIDED rather than written, and both are worth recording because the obvious implementation of each would have needed one. The generation lock several controllers contend for is an os.Mkdir rather than an os.OpenFile with O_CREATE|O_EXCL, which raises no G304 and is additionally the primitive that is unambiguous on the NFS-backed ReadWriteMany volumes this whole fix exists for. The jitter on the retry schedule is crypto/rand rather than math/rand, which raises no G404; it does not need to be unpredictable, only uneven, and the cost of the stronger source once at start-up is a syscall. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-15 by Phase 20c, which made TLS self-provisioning the default: nine waivers, unchanged and unmoved (no guarded line shifted, so nothing needed re-review), and the inline count is still 56. Zero new suppressions, which was not luck: the new internal/tlscert package writes through os.CreateTemp, whose 0600 mode is both what a private key wants and the reason no G306 is raised, and it validates a stored pair through tls.LoadX509KeyPair rather than os.ReadFile, so no G304 arises for the two files it reads back. The one G304 in cmd/controller/healthcheck.go is the SAME suppression Phase 20b added, with its comment reworded to say the path may now also be a self-provisioned certificate; it is not a second one.

waivers.reason: Owned by Phase 11 (API Gateway & Telemetry). This is the SSE stream's "event: init" write, which gosec traces jobID into from a chi URL parameter. Phase 11 closed the underlying risk rather than only waiving it: jobID is rejected unless it parses as a UUID (internal/api/logs.go's StreamLogs, the uuid.Parse guard near the top of the handler), so the value reaching this Fprintf can no longer contain a newline, an angle bracket, or any other character with meaning to an SSE consumer or a browser. The same check closed a real NATS subject-wildcard injection on the subscribe path (FAILURE_PATTERNS.md). gosec's taint analysis cannot see the guard, so the finding remains reported; it is not reachable. Re-reviewed 2026-08-11 (Phase 19): the waiver went stale because this line moved from 135 to 147 when the wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin above it was removed and replaced by a comment explaining why (FAILURE_PATTERNS.md #95). That staleness is the waiver file working as intended -- a finding whose surrounding code moved must be re-reviewed, not silently renumbered -- so the guard was re-read and confirmed present and unchanged before updating the line. The endpoint now also accepts a session cookie, which widens who can reach it but not what jobID may contain. Re-verify at Phase 39.

Owned by Phase 19 (Brutalist UI Scaffold). Handler.setSkin's redirect after recording a theme-family choice. gosec traces the Referer header into http.Redirect and cannot see that Handler.safeReturn constrains it. The underlying risk is closed rather than only re-waived: safeReturn discards rather than validates, parsing the Referer and keeping only its path, so scheme, host, userinfo and fragment are thrown away outright instead of being inspected for something that looks safe. What remains is path.Clean'd, resolving traversal, and then required to be the UI prefix or a path beneath it, so the return value is always a rooted path on this origin. internal/ui/web/safereturn_test.go proves it against 17 real open-redirect techniques including protocol-relative URLs, userinfo hosts, backslash normalisation, traversal, and prefix look-alikes such as /uiadmin. gosec found two genuine defects here before this waiver existed -- an unescaped caller-controlled id reaching path.Join, and an earlier substring-based safeReturn -- both fixed rather than waived. Re-verify at Phase 39. Re-reviewed 2026-08-14 (Phase 79b): the waiver went stale because this line moved when the sign-in handlers were extracted from this file into login.go and writeInsecurePreference's doc comment grew. That staleness is the waiver file working as intended, so the guarded code was re-read before the line was updated: safeReturn and writeInsecurePreference are both byte-identical to what the original review covered, and only their line numbers changed. Re-reviewed 2026-08-15 (Phase 20b): the waiver went stale because this line moved when the development-only insecure cookie writers were deleted from this file and from internal/ui/session, which is the fix Phase 20 was carrying for them rather than an unrelated edit. That staleness is the waiver file working as intended, so the guarded code was re-read before the line was updated: safeReturn and all three appearance handlers are byte-identical to what the original review covered (the diff for this file touches only writePreference's doc comment and the deleted writer), and only their line numbers changed.

Owned by P0 (the AWX parity corpus, .SPECIFICATION/AWX_PARITY_ROADMAP.md). This is the ObjectType constant CredentialTypes = "credential_types", the corpus's name for AWX's /api/v2/credential_types/ endpoint and its testdata subdirectory. G101 pattern-matches the substring "credential" in an identifier and a string literal and flags it as a possible hardcoded secret; there is no secret here, only a resource name this project did not choose (AWX's own). Renaming it would break the stated contract that ObjectType's value is literally the AWX endpoint's plural (this file's own ObjectType doc comment), for no security benefit. Re-verify if this constant's value ever changes to something gosec's heuristic was actually built to catch.

Owned by the template-kind-routing rebuild (FAILURE_PATTERNS.md #112, HANDOFF_ARCHIVE.md's "Phase 21 shipped, the template rebuild" entry), which moved this test-only image builder out of cmd/runner's release gate so tests/e2e could share it. BuildAnsibleRunnerImage runs `docker build -f <dockerfile> -t <tag> <root>`, and G204 flags dockerfile and root as caller-controlled variables reaching exec.Command. Neither is: dockerfile is this package's own repoRoot(tb) plus the fixed, repository-committed literal "Dockerfile.legacy-ansible-runner", and root is repoRoot(tb) itself, found by walking up from the test binary's own working directory until a go.mod is found, never from any external input. This is a testing.TB-gated helper (tb.Helper(), tb.Skip if docker is absent), unreachable from any production binary or network-facing path; gosec's taint analysis has no way to see that "variable" here means "computed by this process from its own module root," not "supplied by a caller."

Owned by Phase 22 (Credential Types & The Injector Engine). This is the ScopeCredentialRead constant, auth.Scope("credential:read"). G101 is a heuristic over identifier and literal text, and it fires here on the word "credential" appearing in both; there is no secret involved. The value is an authorization scope name, the exact string a JWT's "scopes" claim carries, and it is necessarily a compile-time constant for the same reason every other Scope in this file is: the vocabulary is closed, and a typo in a scope literal silently grants a scope nobody holds rather than failing to build. The eleven scopes above it are not flagged only because none of them happens to contain a word gosec's wordlist matches. Reviewed 2026-08-13: the constant holds no credential material and never will, since what it names is a permission to see that a credential EXISTS. There is no endpoint anywhere behind this scope that returns a secret value, which is enforced by internal/archtest's TestAPINeverImportsTheCredentialResolver rather than by review. Re-verify at Phase 39.

Owned by Phase 22 (Credential Types & The Injector Engine). This is the ScopeCredentialWrite constant, auth.Scope("credential:write"). Identical in every respect to the ScopeCredentialRead finding above: a G101 heuristic match on the word "credential" in an authorization scope name, with no secret material present. Two entries rather than one because this file's waivers key on an exact line and each must be re-reviewed individually if either moves. Re-verify at Phase 39.

Owned by Phase 22 (Credential Types & The Injector Engine). This is credentialPrefix, the string "credential_", which is a FORM CONTROL NAME PREFIX and not a credential. It namespaces the launch form's prompted credential inputs, so a control is named credential_<id>_<inputid> and cannot collide with a survey answer's answer_ control or with another bound credential's input of the same name; parseCredentialControl reads the same prefix back off the submission. gosec's G101 heuristic matches the identifier's name against a credential-shaped word list and cannot tell a prefix constant from a secret. There is no secret here to leak: the value is a literal that appears in rendered HTML on purpose, and the actual prompted values are read from the submission at request time and passed to LaunchTemplate as credtype.PromptedInputs, which recordConfig is structurally unable to see. Renaming the constant would silence the finding and would also break the deliberate symmetry with surveyPrefix directly above it in actions.go, which is the pairing that makes the two namespaces legible. Re-verify at Phase 39.
